name: Error Correction Overhead
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Paying for Perfection: The Overhead of Error Correction
lesson.summary: Explains how quantum error correction protects information without directly measuring it, why classical repetition codes cannot be used directly, and the substantial physical qubit overhead this requires.
lesson.body:
The error rate problem covered in the previous section makes clear that raw physical qubits are far too unreliable, on their own, to run the large circuits that algorithms like Shor's would require. Quantum error correction is the technique developed to bridge that gap: it encodes the information of one well protected "logical" qubit redundantly across many physical qubits, arranged so that errors affecting individual physical qubits can be detected and corrected without ever directly measuring, and thereby destroying, the delicate quantum information being protected.

That last requirement is what makes quantum error correction harder than its classical counterpart. A classical repetition code might simply copy a bit three times and take a majority vote, a strategy that works because you can freely read each copy without disturbing it. That approach cannot be used directly on qubits: the measurement problem means directly checking a qubit's value would collapse its superposition, and quantum mechanics additionally forbids copying an unknown quantum state at all. Quantum error correction instead uses indirect syndrome measurements that reveal only what kind of error occurred, without revealing, and therefore without collapsing, the protected logical information itself. The leading practical family of such schemes today is known as the surface code.

This protection comes at a substantial and well documented cost in physical qubits. Encoding a single reliable logical qubit typically requires on the order of one thousand to well over ten thousand physical qubits, depending on the target logical error rate and how reliable the underlying physical qubits already are. Scaling this up to a full algorithm compounds the overhead further. One widely cited engineering estimate, published in 2019 by researchers analyzing the resources needed to factor a 2048 bit RSA key with Shor's algorithm, put the requirement at roughly twenty million physical qubits running for about eight hours, a scale far beyond any quantum computer built to date, which as of this writing top out at a small number of hundreds of physical qubits.

Error correction also only helps once a platform's physical error rate is low enough. Below a so called error correction threshold, adding more physical qubits to the code genuinely and exponentially reduces the logical error rate; above it, more physical qubits just add more opportunities for uncorrected error. Reaching operation below this threshold was for years a major unmet milestone. In late 2024, a prominent research group publicly demonstrated, for the first time, a code where increasing the number of physical qubits measurably decreased the logical error rate, widely reported as confirmation of below threshold operation and an important proof that the theory works as intended on real hardware.

Even with that milestone, the numbers above make clear why fault tolerant quantum computing capable of running the landmark algorithms described earlier in this book remains a future goal, not a present capability. The gap between today's hundreds of noisy physical qubits and the millions that current estimates suggest a cryptographically relevant computation would need is the field's central engineering challenge, and the direct, cumulative consequence of everything in this chapter: fragile qubits, decohering quickly, accumulating errors gate by gate, that must be protected by redundancy at a scale far beyond what exists today.
